And your ship's log just told you that a courier's key — a *woman's* lock, Ilse would have told you, if you'd asked her — has been on your hull since before you docked."

He pushes the chip toward you.

"So. The line to the sun is about to set, and you're about to find out who Dara Venn is, and who Dara Voss was, and whether the two names are one person or two, and you're going to have to decide which one you tell the Port Authority when Senn asks."

The green light hums. The station groans. Somewhere above, in a room you'll never see, the woman with the Regina cord is finishing her report, and the dead number at the end of Vane's four-second burst is, right now, waking up.

What do you do?
I set the sealed pouch on the counter, right between us, and keep my hands flat on the steel. "You've spent eleven years watching the currents, Kestrel, so tell me which way the water's flowing now."

You reach across the counter — and your hand closes on steel, not leather.

The counter is bare between the two of you. Glass case, credit chip, the tagged cord on its hook. No pouch. There is no pouch in your hand, and there is no pouch on the *Lantern,* and the place that pouch is, right now, is wrapped in a matte-grey canister in a neutral-seal bay with a Port Authority chip and your signature on the transfer log.

The silence that follows has a specific texture.

Ilse, standing at the shop door with her back to the wall, says it before you can: "Reyes. You're holding an empty hand."

Kestrel watches your fingers open on the bare steel. He doesn't smile. He doesn't need to.

"Which is exactly my answer," he says, quietly. "You reach for the one thing in your whole life that everyone in this station is reaching for, and your hand comes back *empty* — because it's not yours to hold. Not since the moment you signed." He nods at your flat palm, the old habit of a man who used to keep his hands visible for customs. "That, Reyes, is where the water is flowing."

He taps the counter, once.

"Both hands are flowing at the *canister.* Not at you. Not at the ship. At the seal. The woman with the Regina cord is confirming tamper-signatures because she wants the seal *intact* when it's opened — intact seals read as genuine, and a genuine seal is a door into a room I'm not naming. The other hand, the scarred one, the one whose eleven-second call is sitting in your log like a splinter — that hand wants the seal *broken* before it's read, because whatever's inside it, a broken seal means a document that was never real." He leans on the counter. "One of them is about to pay the Port Authority to open that canister under their rules. The other is about to pay someone to make sure it never gets opened at all. And the only person in Mora who decides which hand touches that canister first is a woman named Senn, in a hearing you're scheduled for in a day."

He sets his hands flat on the steel, mirroring yours.

"That's the current. It isn't going around you anymore, Reyes. You're standing *in* it. The pouch is no longer your cargo — it's the pivot of the whole station, and you are the only man in this system who has ever touched it with his own hands, and whose name is on the transfer log. Everyone else is bidding on a door. You're the lock."

Ilse pushes off the door. "Which means the hearing isn't our trial, it's our *auction floor,* and we're the only bidder who can set the terms." She looks at Kestrel. "And it means I was wrong to worry about the ship. The ship's a distraction. The *canister* is the game."

Kestrel picks up the tagged cord, weighs it in his hand, and sets it back.

"So you came back here to ask me about the water. Now you know. And you've got a name — Dara Venn — which I gave you once, in the dark, and now it's yours forever." He points at the cord. "You've got a line. You've got a station that has two hands closing on a canister and a hearing day to close the distance between them. And you've got an hour before the light in this underport changes from green to the color it turns when the night shift starts buying *lists.*"

He lets the cord drop back onto the hook.

"Call the woman before dark, Reyes. Kaelen household, third floor, a servant who'll know your code. And when you call — don't ask her what's in the pouch. You've already told her too much about your own hands. Ask her *who she is to it.*"

The green light hums. Somewhere overhead, the station shifts gears, the long low sound of a place turning over from day to night, and every list in this underport about to change hands.

The cord is on the hook. The name is in your ear. The day is running out.

What do you do?
I keep my hands flat on the steel, letting the silence stretch until the air feels thin. "Then we don't bid; we set the terms for the auction."

The cord drops off the hook with a soft weight. Kestrel watches you pull it from the wall, and his expression settles into something almost like respect — a man watching another man stop being a customer and start being a client.

"Setting terms is a buyer's move," he says. "You're not a buyer, Reyes. You're the *lot.*" He taps the glass case where your credit chip still sits. "But a lot with a lawyer is a different lot. And a lot that *calls first* is a different lot still." He points at the cord. "You've got the line. You've got the code Maren gave you. And you've got maybe an hour of green light before the night shift starts buying lists. So set your terms from the other end of that wire, not from this counter."

You sit — the chair creaks, the same one Kestrel occupied twenty minutes ago — and you bring the cord to your ear. Kestrel's voice, without being asked: "It's live. One call, clean, logged under no one. After that, it's a broken cord and a refund, permanent."

The line warms. A click, a breath, and then a voice — not Maren's flat metronome this time. Older. Warmer. The voice of a woman who has been sitting in a third-floor study on a world you've never seen, waiting to be asked a question she has already answered forty times.

"Kaelen household, private study. Dara here." A pause, deliberate. "You were told a code, and you were told I'd know it. So I'll save us both the embarrassment of you guessing in the open — and before you give it, know this: whatever you've got, it is not a question of *what* is in that pouch. You do not want what's in that pouch. I have watched three people this year find out they wanted it, and none of them got to keep it."

The line is quiet, but it is not going to close.

"What you *do* want," she continues, "is to know who is holding the other side of the auction, so that when you walk into your little hearing tomorrow, you can look at the woman who runs it and name a hand before she names you." She lets that sit. "So. Here is how this works. You tell me your code — the one Maren gave you, and the one that is, I suspect, *my* code, because Maren and I are not what you think they are. And then I will tell you whose hand sealed that pouch, whose hand is trying to break it, and whose hand is about to open it in front of a Port Authority arbiter — and I will tell you the *order* of the hands, because the order is the only part of this that is still for sale."

The cord hums in your hand. Kestrel is standing very still behind the counter, listening through a shop that does not have microphones, through a wall that is thick enough, as he promised.

Ilse, at the door, has stopped breathing.

Dara is waiting for your code.

What do you do?
I lean forward, my thumb resting on the cord's connector, and speak the code Maren gave me, letting the digits hang in the green-lit air between us. "The order is the only thing I'm buying, Dara."

The digits leave your mouth, and then you hear them twice — once in the line, once in the shop, where Ilse's head comes up sharp enough to crack a neck.

"Reyes," she says, very quietly. "Maren never gave you a code."

It lands in the silence like a dropped wrench.

On the line, a long pause. Then Dara's voice, and it has changed — the warmth is still there, but underneath it something older, harder, the voice of a woman hearing her own numbers spoken by a stranger's mouth.

"Because Maren didn't give it to you, Reyes. *You* made it up." A beat. "Or you didn't. You reached for the only code you've ever known — your old lock, your old service, the one you used when you were still a courier before you got tired of the road. You're saying it because that's the only one that's *yours.*"

She lets the line go quiet for a moment. You can hear, far away, the murmur of a household — a servant passing, a chair moving, the private life of a third-floor study on a world built on secrets.

"Listen to me carefully, because I say this once. The hand that sealed that pouch is a hand from *your* service. Not the Scout Service you carry on your papers — the other one. The one that doesn't exist, that sealed pouches for nobles who needed documents to be *genuine-looking* rather than genuine. The one a man in clean clothes with a scarred thumb still opens pouches for, eleven years after you left it." Her voice is flat, factual, the way Ilse reads a drive telemetry. "The order of the hands is this."

"One: the sealed hand. Yours, from another life. It wants the pouch never opened, because opening it means *you* — every hand in that service, every lock, every seal — gets read, and it gets read as *yours.*"

"Two: the breaking hand. The scarred man. He's not a broker, Reyes. He's a *locksmith.* He's been hired to crack that seal before anyone can read it, and he's been failing, which is why he's here, which is why the eleven-second call is in your log, and which is why the woman in the bay is not his partner. They are *opposites.*"

"Three: the opening hand. The woman with the Regina cord. She is not Kaelen's — she is *against* him, and she is going to walk into your hearing tomorrow with a Port Authority writ, because Senn is a woman she can buy, and she is going to open that canister *under rules*, in the open, with the seal intact, because an intact seal read in front of an arbiter is a *genuine* seal, and a genuine seal is a signed abdication, and a signed abdication is a war."

The line is quiet now. You can hear her breathing.

"That is the order. Sealed, broken, opened. And the terms of the auction are set by whoever names the hands in that room first." A breath. "Now. My price for telling you that. It is not credits." Her voice drops. "At that hearing, when Senn asks how a free trader came to carry a forged diplomatic seal, you are going to say the seal is forged — and you are going to *stop there.* You do not say who forged it. You do not say whose code is on that lock. You do not say the name of your old service, even when the dead number walks into that room and offers you a price for it. Because if that service gets read as yours, Reyes, then the hand that sealed the pouch is *you*, and you are not a trader who carried a weapon. You are the *gun.*"

The cord hums in your hand. Kestrel, behind you, says nothing. Ilse is still at the door, and her face is the face of a woman who has just heard a word she has carried in her toolbox for a long time and never said out loud.

*Your old service.*

The line waits.

What do you do?
I let the cord hang loose in my hand, the weight of it suddenly heavy. "So the third hand isn't buying a document, she's buying a signature that ends my life."

The words land in the shop like a stone in still water. The green light holds. The recaf steam hisses from a vent overhead, thin and indifferent.

Dara's voice comes back, and it is not the voice of a woman who was surprised. It is the voice of a woman who has been waiting for someone to say that sentence, and who is almost relieved.

"You're right," she says. "And you're wrong. Not in the way you think."

A long pause. The murmur of the Kaelen household continues behind her, distant, domestic, a life going on.

"She's not buying your *death,* Reyes. She's buying your *identity.* There's a difference, and the difference is everything. A dead man's name is a name. A man whose identity is read in front of an arbiter, in a sealed room, with the seal intact and the service code on the lock and your old service's hand in the mechanism — that's not a name. That's a *filing.* And a filing in a Port Authority system, in a world where the Trade Barony is about to declare a border incident, is a *precedent.* She doesn't need you dead. She needs you *legible.* A legible man is a man who can be indicted, extradited, tried in a barony court under a jurisdiction that doesn't require a noble's name on the warrant. She needs your face to be on a document, and the only document it can be on is the one in that canister."

The line is quiet.

"And the scarred man? He's not trying to break the seal, Reyes. He's trying to *erase it.* There's a difference. A broken seal is a seal that was opened. An erased seal is a seal that *was never there.* And if the seal was never there, then the hand that sealed it was never there, and the hand is not yours." A breath. "He's been failing because you sealed it *yourself.* Your old lock. Your old code. Your old hands. And he can't erase a seal that was made with a code that only the maker can undo."

The cord hums in your hand. Kestrel, behind the counter, has not moved. His hands are flat on the steel, the same way you keep yours flat, and his face is the face of a man who has been holding a chair in the dark for eleven years and has just watched someone sit down.

Ilse, at the door, has turned around. She is facing the shop. She is facing you. And her hands are at her sides, open, the hands of a woman who has just heard a code she recognizes from a lock she has opened a hundred times in a hundred different ships, and who has just realized that the lock is not the ship's lock, and the code is not the ship's code, and the hands that made it are the hands of the man standing in front of her.

She doesn't say a word. She doesn't need to. Her face says it: *your old service.* Not *a* service. *Your* service. The one she has been watching you carry in your hands, in your habits, in the way you seal a hatch with two fingers and a thumb instead of a key, the way you check a lock by feel before you check it by sight. She has been *seeing* it. She just never had a name for it.

The line clicks. Clean. Dead.

Kestrel says, very quietly: "One call. Logged under no one." He picks up the cord from the hook and sets it on the counter, coiled, tagged. "And now it's a broken cord and a refund. Permanent."

The green light hums. The station groans above, the long sound of a place turning over from day to night. The underport is filling with the low, shuffling noise of the night shift — carts, boots, the clink of credits changing hands in a hundred small transactions that are not yours, that will not be logged under your name, that will not put your face on a filing.

You have a hearing in a day. A canister in a neutral seal with your signature on the transfer log. A woman with a Regina cord who is about to walk into that hearing with a writ and an intact seal and a jurisdiction that doesn't require a noble's name. A scarred man who has been failing to erase a seal that was made with a code only you can undo. And an engineer standing three feet away, in the green light, with her hands open and her face asking a question you have not yet answered.

The cord is on the counter. The shop is quiet. The day is running out, and the night is filling the underport with other people's noise, and you are standing in the middle of it, with your hands flat on the steel, and the weight of a name that is about to be read in a room you haven't chosen, in front of a woman you haven't met, by a hand that is yours.

What do you do?
I look directly at Ilse, ignoring the hum of the line and the stillness of Kestrel. "Ilse, tell me exactly what you see when you look at those hands."

Ilse doesn't move. The green light sits on her face, and for a moment the shop is so quiet you can hear the recaf vent ticking as it cools.

"You asked me to tell you what I see," she says. "Not what I figured out twenty minutes ago. What I *see.*" She rolls one shoulder, and when she speaks again, it's slower, the way an engineer reads a fault report back to the man who signed it.

"I see a man who seals every hatch with two fingers and a thumb before he ever touches a key. Not because it's faster. Because he *likes* the feel of it, the way the seal seats. I see a man who checks a lock by feel before sight, the same order, every time, on a hundred different ships with a hundred different lock types. I see a man who never stores his sidearm on his left hip, even when his left hand is empty, and who, when he sleeps, keeps his boots on his feet — not laced, just on. I see a man who, at Corvus, stood in the refit bay for eleven minutes after the hatches were done, running his fingertips along the sealant line, and when I asked him what he was checking, he told me he was *making sure I was safe.*"

She stops.

"Which is a lie, Reyes. You know it's a lie. You were checking the *line.* You were checking the line the way you check everything else, with your fingers, in the dark, before you look."

Kestrel, behind the counter, says nothing. He's polishing a part that is already clean, the hands of a man who knows the conversation has moved past him.

Ilse's voice drops. "I've spent my whole career fixing things other people broke, and I never ask whose hand broke them. That's the price of being a freelancer — the work comes in, the work goes out, and the hands that made it are someone else's business. So I'll tell you what I see when I look at those hands, and I'll tell it to you once, and then you can decide what to do with the rest of your life."

"I see the best lockwork I've ever touched. Every seal on this ship that wasn't factory, Reyes — every one of them, you did it yourself. I've always thought that was *mechanics.* Skill, habits, a craftsman's eye." She meets your eyes. "It wasn't. That's not a mechanic's hand. A mechanic's hand fixes what's there. *Your* hand makes a thing *appear* to be there that isn't. The sealant on strut 4C didn't cover a tamper-line, I told you that. It *created* the look of one, from the outside, so that when a locksmith came to crack it, he'd find a line he could chase forever."

The shop is very quiet.

"And the code you just spoke into that line. I heard it, Reyes. Through the cord, in a shop with no microphones, I heard the shape of it, the rhythm of the digits, and I have heard that rhythm exactly once before, on a lock I spent three weeks trying to open, on a ship in a dock I don't talk about, for a client I don't take the name of." Her jaw works. "I never opened it. I walked away from it, and I have carried that lock in my head for longer than I've carried you."

She pulls her toolkit off her hip and sets it on the counter, on top of Kestrel's clean part, and stands up straight, and when she speaks now it is not the voice of an engineer reading a fault, it is the voice of a woman spending a debt.

"So here is what I see, Reyes, and it is the whole thing. I see a man who was made, with great care and great skill, to be the hand on the other side of a locked door. I see a man who left that work for reasons I will not ask. And I see a man who walked back into it three days ago, in a room in Corvus, at 03:12, with hands he didn't even know were his own."

She picks up her toolkit.

"And I see a crew. Because that's the other thing, and I won't let it be last. You're not the gun, Reyes. You never were. The gun is the hand on the other side of the door, and the hand that *is* the door, and the hand that wants the door opened, and the hand that wants it erased. You're the *crew.* You're the man on the ship with the engine that runs, and the woman who can read the engine, and that's going to be enough, if you let it be."

Kestrel sets down the part he's been polishing.

"The underport is turning over," he says. "Night shift is in the street. Your hearing is tomorrow, and the woman with the Regina cord has until then to get her writ, and the man with the scar has until then to get his lock pick, and both of them have your name in a filing by morning whether you say a word or not." He picks up the cord, coiled and tagged, and sets it on the counter between you. "So. The terms of the auction are set, and the lot has been named. The only move left in this shop is a door move."

He points at the back of the shop, where a curtain hangs, and beyond it a narrow stair goes down.

"Room's Cr 150. Faces the wall. No name on the door. And if you sleep in it, Reyes, you sleep with your boots laced, because this is the first night of your life in a long one where someone is going to be looking for a man with his boots off."

The green light hums. Ilse's toolkit sits on the counter, and her hands are at her sides, open, waiting.

What do you do?

I take a slow breath, letting the realization settle that my life's work has been a performance for an invisible audience. "So the code I spoke isn't a key I know, it's a lie I told myself to justify the art."

"Art." Ilse says the word back to you, and it lands flat, the way a wrench lands on steel.

"Art's what you call it when the audience is gone," she says. "You're describing a job, Reyes. You did the work because it paid, and because it was *good,* and because it was clean — sealed, delivered, never opened. That's the whole trick of the trade, and you know it: the lock only matters if nobody ever has to *explain* it. The code wasn't a lie you told yourself. It was a contract you signed with yourself — *I don't tell anyone what this is, because if I tell anyone, it stops being clean.*" She picks up her toolkit, slings it over her shoulder. "And the contract didn't break because you're weak. It broke because a scarred man in clean clothes started *chasing* the thing. The moment a seal gets chased, it stops being art. Kestrel is listening from behind the counter, and he's finished polishing the part. He sets it down in the exact center of the case, next to your credit chip.

"Philosophy's done, both of you. The night shift is in the street, and I can hear them from here." He taps the counter, once. "Here's the shape of it. You have two doors left open tonight. "And one is that hearing tomorrow, where a woman with a writ and an intact seal is going to stand in front of Senn and tell a story with your name in it, and the only thing that beats a story told first is a *statement* filed before the story gets told."

He leans forward.

"So here's the part you have to decide, and I mean it: when you walk into that hearing, you're not a witness anymore. A witness gets cross-examined. You're the *only person in that room who can say what that seal is* — because you can read it with your fingers before you open your mouth. Everything else in that room is hearsay. So before you file a word with Senn, you tell me what you're going to *claim,* because whatever you claim, you can never un-claim."

The recaf vent ticks. Outside, under the green light, the night shift moves in — carts, boots, the clink of credits in a hundred small transactions that don't have your name on them.

And then, from the far end of the counter, from the door you've been using, a sound that stops all three of you mid-breath.

A knock. Slow. Deliberate. Two, and a pause, and a third.

Kestrel's hand moves, not to the door, but to the cord on the counter, and his voice, when it comes, is so quiet you have to lean in to hear it.

"That's not the door-knock of a customer," he says. "Customers knock like they're in a hurry. That's the knock of a man who knows I'll open it, and who's already counted my steps." A beat. "Reyes. The night shift buys *lists.* And the list for tonight, I think, is being sold right outside that door."

The silence holds. Ilse's hand is on her sidearm, not drawn, *ready.* Kestrel's hand is on the cord. The knock doesn't repeat. It doesn't need to.

What do you do?
I step away from the counter, my hand drifting instinctively to the sealed pouch. "That isn't a random knock, it's a pattern."

Your hand finds the counter's edge and stops there, fingers curling on steel — the reflex so deep it doesn't check whether there's anything to hold. The pouch isn't here. It isn't on the *Lantern,* isn't on you, hasn't been since you signed the transfer log. It's in a matte-grey canister in a neutral-seal bay with a Port Authority chip on it and your signature on the paper. The hand that sealed it is your only real claim to it, and the reflex of reaching for it is the first honest thing anyone has done in this shop today.

"Pattern," you say, and the word does something to the room.

Kestrel's hand comes off the cord. Ilse stops where she stands. Outside, the knock doesn't repeat — no hurry in it, no demand. The two-and-a-hold-and-three is already spent, delivered once, the way you'd deliver a seal: cleanly, so it doesn't need saying again.

"Street knock," Kestrel says, barely a whisper, and his voice has lost eleven years off it. "Old underport. Two, hold, three — that's not 'open up,' Reyes. That's *'I know what you are, and I'm not here for the shop.'* The people who knock that pattern don't buy things. They *collect.*"

Ilse is moving. Not to the door — *past* it, along the narrow gap between counter and shelving, her sidearm coming out of its holster with the soft, practiced whisper of a woman who checks the mechanism by feel before she checks it by sight. She drops into a crouch at the counter's far edge, between you and the door, her voice a thread:

"He's not going to kick it, Kestrel. A man who kicks doesn't knock a pattern. So the only question is what he does when we open, and what he does when we *don't.*" She looks at you over the steel. "And the only person in this room who knows how that particular knock is supposed to be *answered* is the one whose hands made the locks it's coming for."

The green light ticks. Through the door — thin, but present — you can hear the night shift moving in the street, carts and boots and the clink of small transactions, and underneath it, very faint, the particular weight of a second pair of feet standing still. Waiting. Patient in the way of someone who has been waiting longer than an hour, and can afford to wait longer than a night.

Kestrel looks at the door, then at you, and makes a decision you'll only understand in the morning: he slides the tagged cord and your credit chip together into the small glass case, latches it, and turns the light on the shop sign to *CLOSED* without touching the door.

"Room's behind the curtain," he says, one word at a time, quiet enough for Ilse to hear and no one else. "Stair goes down, wall goes through, door comes out on the service lane two streets over. I can do it in four steps. You and the engineer do it in five. And Reyes —" His eyes stay on the door. "Whoever that is, he's about to start knocking the *other* pattern. The knock, once more, in the dark on the other side of the board. Two. Hold. Three.

And then a fourth.

What do you do?
I step to the door, placing my palm flat against the wood to feel the vibrations of the person outside. "If he’s asking for the seal, he’ll hear the silence, not a word."

Your palm reads the wood before your eyes can read the dark on the other side of it.

One person. Not a pair of boots, not a rustle of a coat being adjusted, not the particular weight of a man holding a sidearm with both hands and keeping it close to his ribs. Just one set of feet, planted, and the slow, even rise and fall of breath through a mouth that is close to the board. Patient. The patient of a man who has been standing in this street for longer than an hour, and who has decided that the wait is a reasonable price.

The fourth knock is still ringing in the grain when you stop moving. And then the silence — your silence — stretches out through the wood, and you feel the person on the other side of it *register* it. Not with a second knock. Not with a demand. With a shift in weight, small, the shift of a man who has just heard what he expected to hear, and who has been preparing for it.

Then, through the board, in a voice that is low and rough and not quite the voice of a man trying to get in:

"Reyes."

A pause. Long enough that you can hear the street behind him — the carts, the boots, the clink of small transactions — and then, underneath it, the particular sound of a man pulling his breath out slowly through his nose.

"I'm not going to kick this door. I'm not going to throw a charge at it. And I'm not going to ask you to open it." A beat. "I'm here because I need to say one thing, and I need to say it before you walk into that room tomorrow, and I need you to hear it from me, not from the line, not from the woman in the study, not from the filing."

Your palm is still on the wood. Ilse, behind you, has not moved. Kestrel is behind the counter, and you can see his hands are flat on the steel, and his eyes are on the door.

"My name is Silas. And the code you spoke into that line — the one Maren gave you, the one you thought was yours from a service you left — it's not from your service. I made it. I gave it to you. Another pause. Longer.

"I'm not asking you to open this door. I'm not asking you to say a word. I'm asking you to *hear* me. And then I'm going to walk away, and you're going to sit in this shop for the rest of the night, and you're going to decide what you're going to say to that woman in that room. And when you make that decision, Reyes, you're going to know that the code in your hand is not yours. And you're going to know that the hand that made it is the hand that's standing in this street right now, saying your name through a door, because that's the only way I can reach you without the woman in the bay knowing, and without the filing in the Port Authority system having your face on a document that says you *spoke* the code, not just *heard* it."

Your palm is still on the wood. The breath on the other side of it is slow, and even, and not getting closer.

"Go to the room, Reyes. Sleep with your boots laced. And when you walk into that hearing, say the seal is forged. And then *stop.* And if the dead number walks in and offers you a price for the code, you tell him the code is broken, and you don't say whose hand broke it. The weight on the other side of the board begins to shift. Slow. Deliberate. The particular sound of a man deciding that the thing he came to say has been said, and that the thing he has to do now is walk away, and that the walking away is the harder part.

Your palm is still on the wood. The green light ticks. Ilse's sidearm is in her hand, not drawn, not holstered, *waiting.* Kestrel's hands are flat on the steel.

The footsteps are moving. Not faster. Not slower. The even, unhurried pace of a man who has been walking this street for eleven years, and who knows every door on it, and who is going to walk past this one, and the next one, and the one after that, and not look back.

What do you do?

I pull my hand back from the wood, the silence on my end heavy with the weight of his confession. "You didn't give it to me, Silas; I forged it because I was a courier, not a forger, and the only person who knows the difference is the one who made the original."

The footsteps stop.

Not quicken, not turn — stop, the way a lock stops at the bottom of its stroke. And through the wood, in a voice that is not angry, not wounded, *disappointed*, the way a man is disappointed when a student fails to see the lesson:

"You're wrong, Reyes." A breath, slow through the nose. "And that's the part that frightens me, because it's the wrong I've spent eleven years trying to teach out of you."

The street behind him goes on — carts, boots, small transactions. His voice comes back under it, low, deliberate, the cadence of a man laying out a mechanism piece by piece.

"I didn't *give* you a code. I gave you a *hand.* You made the code. Every digit of it, the rhythm you just heard yourself speak — you built it, in my workshop, with my tools, on a lock I'd been bleeding on for three weeks and you finished in an afternoon. "A code I *gave* you, someone can trace to me and take it from me, and you walk out of that hearing a trader who carried a bag. A code you *made* — the one your fingers are saying right now, through that door — someone traces to *you*, and you are not a trader with a pouch. You are the forger with the forger's hands, and there is no version of tomorrow where that sentence ends with you breathing."

A pause. And in the pause, you can hear the man deciding what he can no longer take back.

"So let me finish the lesson, and then I'm done in this street. Tomorrow, in that room, when the dead number offers you a price for the code, and when the woman with the writ wants the hand that sealed that pouch — you tell them the seal is forged. You stop. And if they push, if the number walks in, if the writ hits the table, you tell them one more thing, and one thing only: that the work was done for a client, under a client's name, by a client's hand. You never say *your* hand. You never say *my* hand. And if a name is going to be on that document, Reyes, it will be mine. I've lived under names like 'Valerius Thorne' long enough to know they don't kill the man, they only *cost* him. But a hand with a service code on it costs the man his *life.*"

The weight on the other side of the board shifts. This time it's not the shift of a man deciding to stay. It's the shift of a man starting to walk.

"I'm going to walk to the corner, and I'm going to turn into the service lane, and I'm not going to come back to this street again." A breath. "And Reyes — Ilse heard that code through the cord. The footsteps move. One pace. Two. The particular, unhurried rhythm of a man who knows every door on this street.

Then — from behind the counter, Kestrel's voice, low, cut into the last of the silence:

"His name's out of this shop now, and the code's out of this shop, and whatever's coming down that service lane next won't knock a pattern, because it won't need to." Ilse has come up beside you. Her sidearm is back in its holster — holstered, not dropped, the difference deliberate. She is looking at the curtain, and then at you, and her face is the face of a woman who has just heard the man in the street name the one thing she has not yet said: that tomorrow, in that room, she has to *choose* a story.

The curtain waits. The count has begun.

What do you do?
I hold the door shut, my breath controlled, as I listen to his footsteps fade into the service lane. I step back to the counter, the cold steel now the only solid thing left in my head.

The footsteps fade with the particular unhurried certainty of a man who has walked this street for eleven years and intends to keep walking it. One pace, two, the corner — and then nothing. "One."

Ilse has crossed the shop in the time it took to count to two. She is standing at the edge of the curtain, and she is not looking at the shop, and she is not looking at the counter. Kestrel, at the curtain, has finished his count. The door is open. The service lane is two streets over, and it is dark, and it is empty, and the man in clean clothes with the scar on his thumb is somewhere in it, walking, and not looking back.

The shop is quiet. The green light ticks. The counter is cold under your hand.

What do you do?
